Hagarites
HAY-gar-ites
n. pl.
Also Hagarenes in Psalm 83:6; from Hagar, Sarah’s Egyptian handmaid and Ishmael’s mother. A nomadic confederacy of the eastern desert beyond Gilead, they are one of the tribes Scripture reckons as Abraham’s seed after the flesh and outside the covenant.

Definition · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

The Hagarites ranged the desert east of Gilead, and the Chronicler records the war Reuben, Gad, and the half tribe of Manasseh waged against them. The account is short and it is one of the most instructive battle reports in Scripture: they were helped against them, and the Hagarites were delivered into their hand, and all that were with them: for they cried to God in the battle, and he was intreated of them; because they put their trust in him (1 Chronicles 5:20). The next verse adds, because the war was of God. Two and a half tribes who were themselves living east of Jordan by a compromised choice nevertheless prayed in the field and were answered, and the historian will not let the reader attribute the victory to the fifty thousand men who fought it. The Hagarites appear again in Asaph’s psalm among the confederacy plotting against Israel: the tabernacles of Edom, and the Ishmaelites; of Moab, and the Hagarenes (Psalm 83:6). Their name keeps Hagar before us, and Paul makes her an allegory in Galatians 4 — the bondwoman and the free, the son after the flesh and the son by promise. The Hagarites are the flesh’s descendants ranged in arms against the children of promise, which is exactly Paul’s point about the two covenants.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster 1828 has no HAGARITE entry. The Authorized Version uses Hagarites in 1 Chronicles 5 and Hagarenes in Psalm 83:6; both render the same Hebrew, and the name looks back to Hagar the Egyptian.

expand to see more

HAGARITES, HAGARENES, n. pl. — An Arab people of the desert east of Gilead, reckoned as descendants of Hagar.

The two English forms in the Authorized Version render one Hebrew word; the variation is the translators’.

1 Chronicles 5:19 names their allies: Jetur, Nephish, and Nodab — two of the three being sons of Ishmael (Genesis 25:15).

1 Chronicles 27:31 has Jaziz the Hagerite over David’s flocks, so the people were not uniformly hostile.

Webster 1828 does not carry the term; the biblical usage is confined to Chronicles and Psalm 83.

Key Scripture

1 Chronicles 5:10 — "And in the days of Saul they made war with the Hagarites, who fell by their hand: and they dwelt in their tents throughout all the east land of Gilead."

1 Chronicles 5:20 — "And they were helped against them, and the Hagarites were delivered into their hand, and all that were with them: for they cried to God in the battle, and he was intreated of them; because they put their trust in him."

1 Chronicles 5:22 — "For there fell down many slain, because the war was of God. And they dwelt in their steads until the captivity."

Psalm 83:6 — "The tabernacles of Edom, and the Ishmaelites; of Moab, and the Hagarenes;"

Genesis 16:12 — "And he will be a wild man; his hand will be against every man, and every man’s hand against him; and he shall dwell in the presence of all his brethren."

Modern Corruption

1 Chronicles 5:20 is a favourite text of the prosperity teachers, who read it as a formula: trust, and the enemy is delivered. The same chapter ends with these tribes carried away by Assyria for the sin the Chronicler names, which is what a formula cannot survive.

expand to see more

The verse is genuinely a promise-shaped verse — they cried to God in the battle, and he was intreated of them; because they put their trust in him — and it deserves to be preached as one. What must not be done is to lift it out of its chapter. Twenty-six verses later the same tribes are described as transgressing against the God of their fathers and going a whoring after the gods of the people of the land, and God stirred up the spirit of Pul king of Assyria and carried them away. The Chronicler has deliberately set the answered prayer and the captivity in one paragraph. A cry in extremity is heard; it does not purchase a covenant of exemption. Prosperity preaching lives entirely in verse 20 and never reads on to verse 26.

The deeper matter is Hagar herself, and Paul’s use of her in Galatians 4. The bondwoman’s son was born after the flesh, the freewoman’s by promise, and Paul says these are the two covenants. Ishmael was circumcised, was Abraham’s true son, received a real blessing and became a great nation — and was not the heir. That is the sharpest possible statement of the difference between natural descent and sovereign promise, and it is why the Hagarites belong in a Reformed dictionary. Every religion of human effort is Hagar’s child: sincere, energetic, genuinely fruitful in its way, and not the seed to whom the inheritance was given.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew Hagri (H1905), Hagarite, from Hagar (H1904); the confederacy of 1 Chronicles 5:19 is joined with Ishmael’s sons Jetur and Nephish.

expand to see more

Hebrew Hagar (H1904) — Hagar; Sarah’s Egyptian handmaid, Ishmael’s mother (Genesis 16:1).

Hebrew Hagri (H1905) — Hagarite, Hagerite, Hagarene; the desert people reckoned from her.

Hebrew Yetur (H3195) and Naphish (H5305) — Jetur and Nephish, sons of Ishmael (Genesis 25:15) and allies of the Hagarites.

Hebrew atar (H6279) — to entreat, to be prevailed upon by entreaty; he was intreated of them (1 Chronicles 5:20).

Greek Agar (G28) — Hagar; Paul’s allegory of the two covenants in Galatians 4:24-25.

Usage

"They cried to God in the battle, and he was intreated of them (1 Chronicles 5:20) — prayer in the field, answered."

"Because the war was of God (1 Chronicles 5:22) — the Chronicler’s refusal to credit the fifty thousand."

"Of Moab, and the Hagarenes (Psalm 83:6) — the flesh’s children confederate against the church."
